items.body: Review by KansasForEver4 — Scotland's most famous band returns in the early fourth quarter of 2026 with its ninth studio album, "A Song for Tomorrow." It is a soundtrack that traverses the Bible, politics, technology, and the (all-too) many conflicts around the globe to explore what lies behind sensationalist media headlines?namely people, their relationships, their emotions, and their experiences."A Song for Tomorrow" presents the dichotomy between our inner selves and the image we project to the world around us: our dreams, the reasons we get up every morning, our falls and recoveries?everything that ultimately defines the human being.PALLAS has chosen a range of themes encompassing environmental collapse, digital surveillance, fracturing relationships, and the unsettling noises of our daily lives. It is a record that showcases the voices of all four band members on equal footing, with each contributing both lead and backing vocals. Did you like the artwork for "The Messenger"? Rest assured, this one is even better; the liner notes reveal nothing about the current hot topic?AI. Mike Bentley is considered the fifth member of PALLAS.The album opens strongly with "Reset" (9/10)?the shortest track on the record, yet one of true beauty that flows effortlessly. It segues into "Rage," a more muscular, almost metallic, and slightly longer track?a piece where Niall Mathewson proves, if proof were needed, that he is a master guitarist (9/10), delivering a sound reminiscent of a wild, Rush-esque soundtrack. "A Song for Tomorrow"?the title track?features the childlike vocals of Natasha O'Neal (who also collaborates with Niall on other musical projects); it is a very calm track until the 4:34 mark, when it intensifies somewhat in the finale, driven by layered backing vocals (9/10). Next up is the epic "The Private Collector," clocking in at over eight minutes; it places Pallas back at the heart of the symphonic progressive rock style the Scottish quartet has mastered since its early days (revisit "The Sentinel" or "The Wedge"?this track is very close to that sound, perhaps leaning more towards the latter). It is a timeless gem?nothing more needs to be said (10/10).The next two tracks, "Dirt" and "Aspirations," are of similar length and tempo; it is hard to say which I prefer. "Dirt" is more accessible and commercial (reminiscent of certain tracks on *The Cross and the Crucible*), whereas "Aspirations" is gentler, featuring quasi-religious backing vocals and Graeme Murray's twelve-string guitar taking center stage (9/10 for the former, 8/10 for the latter). "Rushing Headlong" is far more frenetic?another short piece, and thankfully so, as it was the only track on the album I genuinely disliked; it is chaotic?a term I sometimes use?and messy (6/10).The final three tracks?comprising a third of the album's total runtime?represent the very best of the symphonic progressive rock genre, of which Pallas has long been a leading light. First is "The Avenue of Broken Dreams," featuring a slow rhythmic build-up, Ronnie Brown's atmospheric keyboards, and Niall Matthewson's guitar work?lyrical, inventive, and tastefully restrained. A musical delight (9/10). Then, the shorter, calmer "Mother" (8/10) serves as a breather before what follows: the concluding track, "Inside Outside." This piece distills the very essence of what has defined PALLAS for decades into just over nine minutes. It is a melodic ascent showcasing the musicians at their peak, featuring the kind of soaring lead vocals and magnificent backing harmonies we love, alongside top-tier symphonic elements (10/10).As a side note, the absence of a real drummer didn't bother me in the slightest; Niall and Ronnie split the percussion programming duties depending on the track. It will be interesting to see how this translates to the stage during the band's final tour in a few weeks, as Alan Reed's illness is forcing the Scottish group to cease live performances.

A risky decision that, despite initial concerns, demonstrated the band's versatility in moving confidently between different musical styles, while leaving fans and critics alike wondering about the direction the band would take in the future.With "Ghost Reveries" (2005), their eighth album, the Swedes once again use death metal as one of the fundamental elements of their sound, integrated with progressive components that are far more developed than in their previous works. Mikael �kerfeldt's demonic growls, the monolithic and dense guitar riffs of Peter Lindgren and �kerfeldt - which evoke extreme bands like Morbid Angel, the more experimental Tool, or the classic Black Sabbath, among others - and a powerful instrumental foundation alternate and blend with deep, clean vocals, crystalline acoustic elements, and Per Wiberg's hypnotic and cosmic keyboards, to construct a sonic tapestry of contrasts and shifts in intensity that moves naturally between ferocity and a hypnotic, enveloping melancholy."Ghost of Perdition", "The Baying of the Hounds" - featuring evocative Jon Lord-style organ - and the oriental-inspired "Beneath the Mire" unfold across expansive instrumental valleys and peaks that showcase the band's maturity, and find their full expression in "Reverie / Harlequin Forest" - featuring superb clean and harmonic phrasing by �kerfeldt - and, above all, in the ritualistic and intriguing "The Grand Conjuration" - reminiscent at times of Pink Floyd's "Echoes" - the album's finest moments.And the influence of "Damnation" is also present and can be felt in the tremulous "Atonement" and "Hours of Wealth," with their keyboards and a certain jazzy flair, and in the closing "Isolation Years," with its acoustic and dreamlike character, featuring �kerfeldt's whispering vocals and Lindgren's arpeggios, ultimately shaping the excellent "Ghost Reveries", one of Opeth's finest albums and standing alongside the iconic "Still Life" and "Blackwater Park".4/4.5 stars

items.body: Mara gets to Germany and does well. She earns, she buys herself a BMW, and what she boasts about is the legroom: now she can spread her legs as far as she likes. Then the car dies on the Autobahn outside Munich. The crisis has eaten her savings, the job has gone and the visa with it, and she is sat in a car she can’t afford to move. “Mara” is the first single from Gastarbeiter, the third album by GORDAN, out on Glitterbeat on 20 November. Singer Svetlana Spajić found the whole story in two lines. A bećarac, ten syllables to a line, the rhyming couplets people trade at weddings and drinking sessions in the Posavina, the farming country along the river Sava in northern Bosnia, one singer calling and another answering back, usually to make a joke or land an insult. Hers was about a woman stuck on the Autobahn in a new car with no money, sending home for someone to come and get her. Spajić wrote the rest. She keeps that couplet running through the whole lyric. Each verse says its line, then says it again with the words swapped round, Mara sliding from the end of the line into the middle. It’s a story being retold, and it gets worse every time. Halfway through, the verb shifts under the repetition and Mara stops whining that she’s been robbed and starts screaming it. By the last verse she’s home in Bosnia with none of the Deutschmarks left, back to the convertible mark, the currency Bosnia brought in after the war and fixed to the German one at one to one. Mara is a gastarbeiter, a guest worker, and there’s a whole tradition of songs about people like her. West Germany coined the word in the 1960s, after Yugoslavia broke with the rest of the socialist bloc and signed a deal to send its workers north, and it stuck in the Balkans as something said behind a man’s back. Those workers sang about missing home, about the shift, about families split by a border and parents left in the village, and that’s the body of song Gastarbeiter takes its name from. On the album sleeve is Gvozden Leaves for Temporary Residence, Mića Popović‘s painting of an ordinary Yugoslav man. Temporary residence was the state’s phrase for going to work in Germany, and Popović, a dissident, put it in the title to mock it. Gordan came together in Berlin during lockdown. Svetlana Spajić brought thirty years of going out to villages across Serbia, Bosnia and Dalmatia, learning the songs from the singers who still hold them, one place at a time, because the next valley sings the same song differently. That work has taken her into projects with Marina Abramović, Robert Wilson and Antony and the Johnsons. Austrian drummer Andi Stecher and German bassist Guido Möbius come out of noise and minimalism instead, and they also work together as GAMS. The three of them made Down in the Meadow for Morphine Records in 2021 and a self-titled album for Glitterbeat in 2024. In its own album notes, the band describes “Dark Bellow” as a dive into “instinct, desire, fear, betrayal, and rebirth,” moving through the “suffocating ghosts of hidden emotions” before closing on what the notes call “the velvet nostalgia of another life.” About Vioflesh Vioflesh formed in Santiago, Chile, at the end of 2017. The duo works across coldwave and synthpop. darkTunes Music Group signed the band and released its debut album, “Nostalgia,” digitally on 9 May 2025. Young And Cold Records handled the vinyl edition, and Vioflesh issued its own CD and cassette pressings. The band played US dates this October, including Seattle on 17 October, Portland on 21 October and San Francisco on 22 October. items.body: People leave, and time has the appalling manners to keep moving. A night of company gives way to an empty morning; the room that briefly felt habitable becomes a place for counting what has gone missing. For Obychno Odyn, that familiar collapse belongs to a much larger uncertainty, where even the smallest assurances of affection or stability can disappear before we have learned to trust them. The Turin-based coldwave and post-punk project of Ukraine expat Vadym Protsenko explores that precarious existence on the new single “Уходят люди и часы”, a title that can be translated as “People and Hours Pass.” Its accompanying video, premiering here, takes the song’s profound isolation outdoors, into tall grass, wooded paths, and the dark recesses of old stone ruins. A crunchy snare beat marches through a wash of windlike white noise before the bass establishes its brooding, melodic pattern. There is something almost reassuring about that low-end repetition, a foothold beneath a guitar line intent on making the ground uneven. Fuzzy and discordant, the guitar bends into a jagged melody with the pinched, wayward quality of an out-of-tune saxophone. Protsenko’s voice hangs farther back, its ghostly contours extended by cold reverb, as though the words have traveled across an empty building before reaching us. It makes an appropriately spectral opening to October, with enough rhythmic insistence to keep despair on its feet. The Russian-language lyrics describe a life in which direction and meaning are gradually becoming illegible. People and hours depart together, leaving little beyond the silent business of passing time. A burning planet continues to turn while everyone attends to their own concerns; words are thrown away, and even home offers no guarantee of freedom. Against that wider devastation, the possibility of being needed becomes a modest, painfully temporary refuge. The closing lines, translated into English, bring that feeling into focus: “Sometimes, we are needed by someone Sometimes, at night, we are not alone. But then the morning comes And once again, there is not a soul nearby” That repeated “Sometimes” allows a little tenderness into the song, then measures how briefly it lasts. Morning brings the return of the same absence, sharpened by having been interrupted. The bleakness comes from knowing that closeness is possible while having no confidence that it will remain. The video gives that uncertainty a grainy, unsettled physical presence. Guitar and bass performances alternate between daylight beneath the trees and murky passages enclosed by masonry. Close-ups catch faces through branches and long grass; elsewhere, the image turns upside down, briefly dislodging the performers from solid ground. The greenery crowds the frame, making these open spaces feel surprisingly secluded. There is an appealing awkwardness to the musicians’ black clothes against all that growth, as though they have brought the emotional temperature of an empty club into the middle of the afternoon. Watch the video for “Уходят люди и часы” below: Protsenko founded Obychno Odyn in Bucharest in 2025, responding to global upheaval and the situation in his home country. Writing in Russian and English, he draws on the French coldwave of the 1980s, particularly Trop Tard and Bunker Strasse. The eight-song debut album Излияние (Outpouring) followed in 2026, alongside the project’s first live performances in Bucharest, with DJ sets by Corina Sucarov. The solo project expands into a duo onstage: Protsenko handles vocals and guitar, joined by bassist Marcello Aloisio, who became part of the live lineup this year. “Уходят люди и часы” is available now on streaming platforms. items.body: Deathrock has always had a practical relationship with bad news. A macabre sense of mortality supplies the subject matter, punk supplies the impatience, and everyday life keeps renewing the subscription. East Bay four-piece Normal Weirds bring those concerns together on Frown Time, a title that sounds reasonably restrained given the circumstances. Released October 2, the band’s second full-length gathers ten songs that push further into deathpunk and deathrock while retaining their anarcho-punk roots and post-punk unease. The band’s own description, “deathrock gloom dragged through the dirt of punk,” gives a useful indication of the record’s priorities: atmosphere, abrasion, and the urgency of having something unpleasant to get off your chest. Normal Weirds released their debut album, Same Difference, in 2024, followed by the six-song EP No Lease On Life in 2025. The debut examined growing up and working free of the circumstances that had already laid out a person’s future. Taken alongside that earlier record, Frown Time suggests a widening field of concern, with individual frustration meeting the larger sense that the whole arrangement is becoming increasingly fucked. Driving basslines and hard, direct drums provide the foundation, with guitars moving between wiry punk attack and darker passages thickened by effects. Urgent, sometimes theatrical vocals heighten the unease, while lean arrangements preserve the roughness of the band’s approach. The emphasis stays on noise, tension, and the force of the playing, giving their darker direction a distinctly physical edge. The band offers Rudimentary Peni, Cemetery, T.S.O.L., and Chain Cult as points of comparison. “Deathpunk” feels like a useful shorthand for the territory they describe, where punk aggression and deathrock atmosphere share the same cramped quarters. Across their releases, Normal Weirds have increasingly brought those impulses together, giving the darker material a harder and more direct frame. Mortality, alienation, and everyday absurdity run through the album’s lyrical concerns. Its ominous mood draws on both personal experience and a broader disillusionment with the present. There is a bluntness to the title that suits that outlook: Frown Time makes room for the irritation and apprehension people are often expected to swallow while getting on with their day. Frown Time was recorded, mixed, and produced by Skot Brown of Altar De Fey and mastered by Greg Wilkinson. The album is available to stream and purchase on Bandcamp here. It will be released on other streaming platforms, excluding Spotify, on October 16, 2026. items.body: Somewhere between the panic attack and the curtain call, Fiona’s Phobias have found a rather entertaining place to set up shop. Their six-track EP DEMOnS Vol. 1 dresses burnout, self-disgust, and impossible attachments in gothic metal, pop punk, and dark cabaret, with enough theatrical excess to suggest that the orchestra pit has opened directly into hell. The jokes have teeth, the guitars favor elaborate flourishes, and the people inside these songs keep discovering that their favorite distractions have become further reasons to worry. Formed in 2022, the project pairs the deliberately elusive Nikki L with vocalist Krisanna Marie, whose background includes Hatesex, Penis Flytrap, and burlesque fire Go-Go performance. Their own comparison of the working relationship to The Phantom of the Opera seems appropriate for music so fond of trapdoors and dramatic entrances. Marie’s ability to move from a knowing, almost conversational delivery into operatic gestures gives these elaborate arrangements a useful center: someone has to keep an eye on the audience while the scenery catches fire. Euphoria is Tragic starts with a chugging guitar figure planted between punk and metal, while Marie brings a retro rock directness to its catalogue of procrastination and depleted pleasure. Around the minute mark, the arrangement grows dense with baroque embellishment; a wiry solo takes on something of an electric violin’s bite. The bright momentum makes an effective companion to lyrics about getting bored with your own bad habits. “I feel my powers wane; a witch without her magic” supplies the perfect image for that particular exhaustion, when yesterday’s magnificent escape becomes today’s inability to answer an email. The theatrical scale expands on Play It Cool, which sets an almost lounge-like opening vocal against metal accents before breaking into a gallop. There is something of Malice Mizer’s baroque grandeur in the meeting of ornate arrangements and vocal melodrama, with the forward motion suggesting the carriage from Castlevania: Rondo of Blood racing toward Dracula’s front door. Beneath the spectacle lies a grimly familiar instruction: take your pill, eat your food, behave, and convince everyone that nothing is wrong. As Marie’s singing becomes more operatic, the pressure to appear composed turns increasingly sinister, eventually spilling into the song’s bloodied escape fantasy. Imaginary Sins brings piano, nimble bass, and busy drums into a crooked little cabaret before the heavier ornamentation takes over. Guitar flourishes answer the rhythm’s clipped figures, and goblin-like responses jostle Marie’s lead, as though every unwanted thought has secured a speaking part. Its funniest lyric finds the bodily absurdity inside a familiar wish: “Wishin’ I was pretty on the inside – But there’s just guts.” Jealousy, appetite, and self-absorption populate this ballroom of dancing demons, while the music’s constant activity makes obsession feel exhausting even at its most playful. The cover of Bang Bang, offered as an ode to Kill Bill, fits neatly among these accounts of love going horribly wrong. A Phantom-style organ opening and old-school metal guitar melody send the song toward the grand, charging territory of Bonnie Tyler’s Holding Out for a Hero. Its childhood games and adult abandonment acquire the dimensions of a stage tragedy, complete with an ornate guitar solo. Placed between the EP’s psychological grotesques, the familiar tune becomes another example of affection leaving somebody flat on the floor. Whispers and giallo-like synth tones introduce She Loves To Kiss That Doll, before sweeping guitars open the room around Marie’s voice. An operatic interlude, edged with chimes, suspends the heavier movement as she sings of attachment to a figure whose beauty depends on a terrible act of denial. Stuffing, cold hands, and the replacement of blood with a handsome face turn romantic idealization into physical horror. The return of the metal arrangement gives that revelation force, while the lyric’s eventual admission that he has long been dead makes the tenderness more disturbing than any decorative cobweb could manage. Closing track Bittersweet Darling begins with chilly piano and the worn texture of an old recording, then carries that melodic idea into a broad sweep of gothic guitar. Progressive tempo changes unsettle a romance conducted through black-and-white television images, broken mirrors, and the comfort of a boxed-up illusion. Its lover remains available because the screen can keep performing; the person watching has surrendered something harder to recover. By the final turn toward the knife and the closing credits, the song has brought the EP’s appetite for spectacle into uncomfortable proximity with self-destruction. Across DEMOnS Vol. 1, the sheer amount of decoration can crowd the stage, but Marie’s shifts in delivery and the songs’ sharply drawn situations keep the excess purposeful. Fiona’s Phobias are especially effective when a grotesque image exposes an ordinary humiliation: craving attention while avoiding people, mistaking possession for love, or spending all your energy on the thing that leaves you empty. They have given those contradictions a lavish production, and the casting department appears to have found plenty of monsters willing to sing. DEMOnS Vol. 1 is out now, released October 2 via Misophoniac Rabbit. Listen below and find the EP on Bandcamp and Spotify. items.body: Même Soleil is a new release from IIKKI, consisting of a dialogue between French musician Frédéric D. Oberland and French photographer Gaël Bonnefon. The collaboration was initiated by IIKKI in December 2019 and concluded in June 2021. On Même Soleil, and as in previous IIKKI incarnations, image and sound coalesce, but the joining of the two mediums produces so much more than the sum of their own parts. When they meet at the intersection, you can expect the two contrasting artforms to explode in a fiery collision. This record offers up a spicy dialogue, a deep and pervading contrast between light and darkness, the two differing genders represented through its music and photography. Même Soleil sees multi-instrumentalist Oberland in fine form. The music spirals into an uninterrupted stream of complexity, high detail, and originality; an ongoing battle between heaving dissonance and harmonic breakthrough. Despite its sketchy underworld, Oberland concentrates on narrative and drives the music forward with a real sense of momentum, keeping it on a barely-visible road that’s been littered with effects pedals and dark-glowing synths, but also infused with jazz-inspired, sharp-edged horns. Grainy, broken-up recordings of discussions and arguments on late night TV are beamed through and broadcast via the music, signalling the hour of midnight, and there’s no doubt that Oberland’s music favours the dark. On this record, the aim was to ‘merge mystical visions of the unconscious and the absurdity of an apocalyptic present in a sensory whirlwind’, and Oberland’s music goes deep enough to encounter those exotic regions and inner psychological temples, as well as its outer world and its interactions with it. The two mediums strain against one another, and this can be felt as much as heard, a living tension existing between the brilliance of daylight and the infinite bliss of a night sky. www.iikki-books.com

items.body: ‘Blue Canyon’, by Michael A. Muller (co-founder of Balmorhea), will be releasing a new EP on December 1. Concerned with the specific isolation of wilderness and arriving just in time to take in the snowy elements of the winter season, Blue Canyon offers a respite from the world, thanks to its still and subdued piano. Conceived just before the global pandemic and releasing in the wake of the US presidential election results, the music is a chance to exhale after months of turbulence and unrest. Created during an artist residency at Laity Lodge, in Real County, Texas, which is described as ‘a rugged property down a near-mile drop in elevation in the cedar and caliche wilderness’, Blue Canyon was recorded in purposeful isolation. Although it was recorded in March – a week before the enforced nation-wide lockdown – it could have come from a different era, when the word ‘isolation’ didn’t have the capacity to provoke a panic attack. Muller stayed at the lodge, alone, creating music to fit into and coalesce with the confines of his environment, both spatially and figuratively, intentionally isolating himself within the beauty of the Frio River canyon. He chose to immerse himself in a state of seclusion and isolation, rather than being forced into it by governments, laws, and stay-at-home orders. Nine months later, some people may turn their heads at the thought of having to be alone. But this was not a barricade, or a makeshift prison. It was a chance to be alone – physically, at least, being present among the beauty of nature while retreating from the wider world. Using a Steinway & Sons grand piano and two microphones, Blue Canyon strips everything away – all but the essential. In this way, the music is like a hard reset, providing a sliver of kindness in sketchy times. Choosing facts over illusion and deep, meaningful notes over disinformation and needless clutter, the music is a relief among uncertainty. In fact, the metronomic rhythm, created entirely from the body of the piano, is an assurance, a continuing certainty that relieves pressure and worry and stress. Its incredibly brief nature (the two pieces add up to a total running time of five minutes, making it the shortest record we’ve reviewed) is a sign of the times, with its escapism running into real-world distress as the five-minute-mark comes to an end, but it’s able to feel like a short-but-effective meditation, and exactly what a breather should feel like. On reflection, it’s the perfect length. Any longer and the record would lose its purpose, as well as its strength. There’s a sense of desperate relief in the music – a feeling of breakthrough and the clarifying power of rest. Clarity is a key component of the music. Muller’s largely improvised music was recorded in between solitary hikes through the canyon, and ‘birdwatching at dusk with the soft sway of 100-foot cypress trees rustling in the distance.’ On the final evening of his residency, a thunderstorm broke loose. Sheets of rain and a roaring wind threw echoes at the limestone cliffs. After a storm, though, the air feels cleansed. Blue Canyon feels cleansed, too. It’s the sound of sunshine breaking through and extinguishing a deluge of rain. www.michael-muller.com

items.body: I’m not very familiar with the work of Dick Raaijmakers, the electronic music pioneer who created numerous groundbreaking works of electroacoustic music and music theatre. Listening to his compatriot Thomas Ankersmit’s homage to the great Dutchman, I’m struck by how many of the sounds generated by Ankersmit’s Serge Modular synthesiser resemble the sounds of war: explosions of fuzz, rapid rotating like helicopter blades, machine gun spitting of dirt, thick burning noise… I’d listened a few times before I read that Raaijmakers would’ve been nine years old at the time of the Battle of Maastricht, when Nazi Germany attacked and captured the city of his birth. I’m not sure how relevant this connection is, if indeed there is a connection. Perhaps Ankersmit would point instead to the ways in which the quirks of analogue electronics lead directly to some interesting aesthetic and psychoacoustic effects. Consider, for example, the rapid beepings heard maybe a third of the way through the piece: they interfere with and stumble over one another in ways that are strangely disorienting to listen to. Imprecision and timing errors are here not effaced or swept under the carpet, but rather taken advantage of to create novel sensory experiences. Towards the end of the piece, a two-pitch seesawing pattern and a buzzing that shifts and grows in bandwidth create an unstable, curiously vague impression, an intensity that presses from all points and none. But it’s hard to get over the sense of chaos and even violence that erupts in the middle of the piece, spewing fire and thunder in all directions. It’s hard to detach oneself from its terrorising effect on base instinct in order to perceive the psychoacoustic phenomena at work. And maybe that’s not the point, as Raaijmakers’ interest in theatre, that art form most invested in the suspension of disbelief, suggests. In any case, “Homage to Dick Raaijmakers” is a spectacular, cacophonous tribute to a trailblazer of electronic music, with Ankersmit’s own careful attention to structure and pacing very much in evidence. It’s certainly piqued my curiosity in Raaijmaker’s work and legacy.
